title_en: Historic Bridge Reopens After Eight-Year Restoration
title_ru: Исторический мост открыт после восьми лет реставрации
description_ru: Вымышленная новость об открытии отреставрированного викторианского моста в городе Харроуфорд: споры, перерасход бюджета и надежды горожан.
text:
HARROWFORD - Thousands of residents lined the banks of the River Alden on Saturday morning to watch the Marlowe Bridge reopen to traffic after an eight-year restoration that has cost nearly forty million pounds, almost double the original estimate.

The ceremony, delayed by half an hour owing to a stubborn thunderstorm, was led by the mayor, Councillor Ingrid Pelham, who cut a ribbon of green silk before walking across the span at the head of a brass band. "This is more than a piece of engineering," she told the crowd, many of whom had waited since dawn beneath umbrellas. "It is a promise kept to a town that refused to forget its own history."

Completed in 1871, the Marlowe Bridge was long regarded as a masterpiece of Victorian ironwork, its elegant arches carrying carts, trams and, eventually, lorries across the river for a century and a half. By the 2010s, however, inspectors had found serious corrosion in the supporting beams, and in 2017 the council reluctantly closed the structure to everything except pedestrians. A heated debate followed. Some councillors argued that the bridge should be demolished and replaced by a cheaper concrete crossing, while a vocal campaign led by local historians insisted on full restoration.

The campaigners eventually prevailed, helped by a substantial grant from a national heritage fund and by a series of public donations that included a single anonymous gift of two hundred thousand pounds. Work began in 2018 but was repeatedly hampered by unforeseen complications. Engineers discovered that the original foundations had been weakened by decades of erosion, and a prolonged spell of flooding in 2021 halted operations for nearly a year. The cost rose steadily, provoking criticism from opposition members, who described the project as a monument to poor planning.

"Nobody pretends it went smoothly," conceded Dr Samuel Okafor, the chief engineer, who has overseen the work since its inception. "But I would ask critics to remember that we were repairing something that was built without computers or modern steel. Every rivet had to be examined individually, and about a fifth of them had to be replaced by hand-forged copies. You cannot hurry a job like that without regretting it later."

The craftsmanship involved became something of a local fascination. A team of six blacksmiths, working in a converted warehouse on the eastern bank, produced more than nine thousand replacement rivets, heating each one to a glowing orange before hammering it into place while still hot. Visitors were invited to watch from a viewing platform, and a school programme brought some four thousand children to the site over the years. "I told my class that the bridge was older than their great-great-grandparents," said Tobias Wren, a primary school teacher. "They were astonished that anything made of iron could survive that long, as long as someone looks after it."

The restored bridge retains its original character, but with several discreet improvements. A reinforced deck can now bear vehicles of up to eighteen tonnes, a separate cycle lane has been added, and a subtle lighting system will illuminate the arches after dark. Buses will resume their regular route across the river from Monday, ending a detour that commuters say has added up to twenty minutes to their daily journeys.

Not everyone was in a celebratory mood. Councillor Desmond Faulk, who led the opposition to the project, argued that the sum spent could have funded a new primary school and a health centre. "I admire the ironwork as much as anyone," he said, standing at the edge of the crowd, "but a town has to decide what it can afford, and I am not convinced that a handsome bridge is a better use of public money than a new classroom." Councillor Pelham, asked about the criticism, replied that the grant from the heritage fund could not have been spent on schools, and that the bridge would pay its way in tourism.

Local business owners, at least, have welcomed the news. "The reopening could not have come sooner," said Marguerite Dunn, who runs a bakery near the eastern end of the bridge. "We lost a third of our customers when it closed. I think people are going to celebrate with cake." By midday, she reported, her shelves were already half empty, and she had sent her son to buy more flour.

Experts say the Marlowe Bridge may prove a model for other towns with ageing infrastructure. Professor Lena Hartmann, who teaches civil engineering at a university in the north of the country, said that Britain has hundreds of similar Victorian structures nearing the end of their working lives. "The temptation is always to demolish, because it looks cheaper on paper," she said. "What Harrowford has shown is that a proper restoration costs more upfront but leaves you with an asset of enormous cultural value. The real question is whether other councils will be as stubborn as this one."

The council has announced that a small exhibition about the bridge's history will open in the old toll house next month, and that an annual lantern festival will be held on the span every autumn. In the meantime, residents are encouraged to enjoy a bridge that, after nearly a decade, is once again part of the town's daily life. As the last of the umbrellas folded and the band struck up a final march, one elderly spectator was heard to remark that she had waited eight years to cross it and intended to do so again, twice, before lunch.
